opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more interesting directions right now, and honestly one I've been thinking about for a while. The traditional way we've done retrieval is this pipeline: you have an index, you have some kind of encoder, maybe a dual encoder, you do nearest-neighbor search, and then you hand the results to a reader or a ranker. Each piece is engineered somewhat separately.

What's exciting is the question of how much of that can be folded into the model itself. That was part of the motivation behind the Differentiable Search Index work: what if the model just memorizes the corpus and learns to map a query directly to a document identifier? You don't have a separate index; the parameters *are* the index. It was a fairly provocative idea, and there are obviously lots of open problems, like how you update the corpus without retraining, or how it scales to really large collections. But I think it pointed at something real, which is that these models are surprisingly good at storing and recalling information when you set up the objective correctly.

At the same time, I'm pretty pragmatic about it. In practice today, retrieval-augmented setups, where a model calls out to some external search and then reasons over the results, are really effective. Long context has also changed the picture a lot. When you can stuff a huge amount of text into the context window, the boundary between "retrieval" and "just reading" gets blurry. So the interesting question isn't really whether language models will be used for retrieval, because they already are, but where the right boundary sits between what lives in the parameters, what lives in the context, and what lives in an external system.

My general bias is that things tend to get absorbed into the model over time. A lot of what used to be bespoke pipelines eventually becomes something one big model just does end to end. But retrieval has practical constraints, like freshness, attribution, and cost, that make it a bit stickier than other tasks. So I'd expect a hybrid for quite a while, with the model taking on more and more of the work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've actually spent a lot of time thinking about, because retrieval and language models were kind of separate worlds for a long time, and now they're converging in a way that I think is really interesting.

The classic view of retrieval is that you have an index, you have documents, you embed them or you build an inverted index, and then at query time you go fetch the nearest neighbors. That's a very mechanical pipeline. The model is just an encoder; it's a feature extractor. And for a long time that was the right design, because models were small and you couldn't afford to put the whole corpus inside the model.

What's changed is that these models have gotten good enough that you can start asking: do we even need the index as an external thing? That was really the motivation behind the differentiable search index work, DSI, which we did at Google. The idea was, what if the model itself is the index? You train it to map a query directly to a document identifier. It sounds a little crazy, but it works surprisingly well on smaller corpora, and it reframes retrieval as just another sequence-to-sequence problem. Retrieval becomes generation.

Now, I want to be honest about the limits. Scaling that to billions of documents is hard. You run into issues with updating the corpus, with memorization capacity, with hallucinated identifiers. So I don't think the external index goes away anytime soon. What I think happens instead is that the boundary gets blurry. You have models that are doing retrieval-ish things internally through their parametric knowledge, and then you have external retrieval augmenting them, and the question becomes how you allocate between the two.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of what people call "retrieval" now is really reranking or reasoning over retrieved content. The first-stage retrieval is still often pretty dumb, like BM25 or a dense embedding model, and then the language model does the heavy lifting on top. That's actually a very sensible division of labor. Cheap, recall-oriented retrieval first, then an expensive model that's good at reading.

Long context complicates this too. If you can stuff a hundred thousand or a million tokens into the window, some retrieval problems just become reading problems. But that's not free, and I don't think long context replaces retrieval. It changes what you retrieve. You retrieve bigger chunks, you retrieve less precisely, and you let the model sort it out.

So my overall view is, I'm pretty bullish on it, but I think the interesting work isn't "replace retrieval with an LLM." It's rethinking what retrieval even means when the thing consuming the results is a model that can read and reason, rather than a human scanning ten blue links.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really interesting direction because retrieval is fundamentally about understanding what someone is looking for, and that’s not always captured by matching words. Language models give us a way to connect a query with relevant information even when they’re expressed very differently.

But there are different ways to use them. You can use a model to generate representations for retrieval, to rewrite queries, or to rerank the documents you’ve already found. Those choices have very different costs and latency tradeoffs. A more capable model isn’t automatically a better retrieval system if it makes every query prohibitively expensive.

The question I find interesting is how tightly retrieval and generation should be coupled. Retrieving something that looks relevant is one thing; retrieving the evidence you actually need to answer a question is another. I think there’s a lot of room to improve that connection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really interesting direction. Retrieval is fundamentally about understanding what someone is asking for and matching that to useful information, so language models have a natural role to play. You can use them to represent queries and documents, rerank results, or even generate the identifiers of documents directly.

But I think the important question is where that extra modeling power actually helps. Retrieval has pretty demanding constraints around latency, cost, and keeping information up to date. A larger model might give you better relevance, but you still have to make the whole system practical. So I’m excited about the possibilities, especially systems that combine efficient retrieval with more expressive models for the harder parts.
